narration: The Silent Bells of Melattur
This is Melattur style. 20th century.
on_screen: Title card: Melattur style · India · 20th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The style was developed by Mangudi Dorairaja Iyer (1900–1980), a sanyasi and practitioner of Srividya Upasana.
He drew inspiration from the devadasi traditions of the Cheyyur Sengalvarayar temple and the Melattur Bhagavata Mela.

Iyer was particularly moved by a devadasi performance featuring 72 different types of items, leading him to re-establish rare forms like Suddha Nrittam, Bhattasa Natyam, and Perani Natyam within the Bharatanatyam framework.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The style is deeply spiritual, rooted in Srividya Upasana.
It rejects the glorification of human patrons, focusing exclusively on deities and rishis.
The use of sringara rasa (erotic/romantic love) is common, reflecting the devadasi influence, but it is channeled toward a spiritual or devotional context rather than a neutral bhakti.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by large-amplitude movements and a wide range of tempos.
Footwork is sophisticated; dancers avoid stamping hard, instead using ankle bells to produce varied rhythmic sounds.
It features extensive use of pancha nadais and gati bhedas, with rhythmic shifts occurring frequently, such as in every jati of a varnam.
Watch for Suddha Nrittam, Perani Natyam.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Soloist moving across a wide scale; uses both loka dharmi and natya dharmi.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music follows the Carnatic tradition typical of Bharatanatyam but emphasizes complex rhythmic structures like pancha nadais.
The salangai (ankle bells) are treated as a musical instrument in their own right, used to highlight intricate rhythms through controlled tapping rather than forceful striking.
Listen for the Mridangam, Nattuvangam (cymbals), Flute, Violin.
The pulse is Complex (extensive use of pancha nadais).

The sound is defined by the sophisticated use of ankle bells which produce a rich variety of rhythmic tones without the thud of hard stamping. The music follows Carnatic structures but is marked by frequent and complex shifts in gait and time measures.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear the traditional Bharatanatyam costume but with a specific addition: a special protective cotton belt worn around the waist to support the body during demanding movements.
The setting is traditionally the temple or the village square of Melattur, though it is now performed on modern stages.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Mangudi Dorairaja Iyer is the central figure who codified the style.
He was a sanyasi whose spiritual practices dictated the themes of the repertoire.
The style is a specific regional variant of Bharatanatyam originating from the village of Melattur in Tamil Nadu, India.
The lineage flows from the temple devadasi traditions and the Melattur Bhagavata Mela through Mangudi Dorairaja Iyer to his students.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Melattur style is parent of Bharatanatyam: Melattur is a specific style or school within the broader Bharatanatyam tradition.
Melattur style is influence of Kuchipudi: Shares elements like Suddha Nrittam and Perani Natyam (clay pot dance).
Melattur style is influence of Bhagavata Mela: Provides the dramatic characterization and abhinaya elements.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The repertoire is strictly limited to the glorification of deities and rishis; items praising human patrons are excluded due to the founder's Srividya Upasana spiritual practice.
